name: Haematopoietic stem cell
markers: No lineage markers (none of CD3, CD19, CD14 or CD15; tells it apart from mature cells)
summary: A rare cell in the bone marrow that can renew itself and make every kind of blood cell, from red cells and platelets to neutrophils and B cells. Most rest quietly beside blood vessels and divide only now and then. In mice, daily blood production seems to come mainly from their daughters. Bone marrow transplants depend on these cells.
functions: Self-renews: when it divides, it can make another stem cell, so the pool is kept up for life. Most stay at rest for long periods; in mice the most dormant divide only a few times in a lifetime. Rates in people are estimated indirectly and are less certain.

Gives rise to all blood cells in steps. Its daughters first become multipotent progenitors, then progenitors limited to fewer cell types, which divide many times and mature into red cells, platelets, granulocytes, monocytes, dendritic cells, mast cells, B cells and NK cells. Early T-cell progenitors leave for the thymus to finish.

Stays in its niche through signals from nearby stromal and endothelial cells: stem cell factor (SCF) binding c-Kit, and the chemokine CXCL12 binding CXCR4, which holds it in place. Work on these signals is mainly in mice.

Debated: where the main niche is. Studies in mice place most resting stem cells beside the sinusoids, others near arterioles, and the two views have not been reconciled. Human niches are much less well mapped.

Debated: how the family tree branches. The textbook model splits the tree into common myeloid and common lymphoid progenitors. Single-cell studies of human marrow suggest the lineages separate earlier and in more routes than that.

Debated: how much it contributes to everyday blood production. Tracking studies in mice found that, in the steady state, most new blood cells come from multipotent progenitors, with stem cells acting as a slow reserve. Their output rises after infection, bleeding or chemotherapy.

Moves between marrow and blood: a few stem cells leave the marrow, circulate and return, shown in mice. G-CSF, or drugs that block CXCR4, drive many into the blood, which is how stem cells are collected for transplants.
Rebuilds the whole blood and immune system after it is destroyed, as in bone marrow or stem cell transplants. In mice, a single stem cell can do this.

Changes with age: stem cell numbers rise but they make more myeloid cells and fewer lymphocytes, and mutations that give one stem cell a growth advantage can let its descendants take over the blood (clonal haematopoiesis).
abundance: Very rare. In mice, roughly 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 100,000 bone marrow cells has stem cell markers. In people, CD34-positive cells are roughly 1-3% of bone marrow cells, but most of them are progenitors, so true stem cells are far fewer. Normal blood holds very few.
